note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

unit.title: Fault find and repair/rectify basic electrical circuits and secondary wiring

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: An operator at a packaging plant in Kingston says a conveyor 'stops by itself now and then'. What should you do first?
options: Replace the motor contactor, because contactors wear out over time
Gather the facts: when it stops, any alarms, and its history
Fit a larger overload relay so that it stops tripping
Ask the operator to restart it each time it stops

questions.stem: Which drawing is best for following the logic of a control circuit, line by line?
options: The panel layout drawing showing where parts are mounted
The site plan drawing showing the building and roads
The cable route drawing showing trays and conduits
The schematic (ladder) diagram

questions.stem: Which drawing tells you the terminal number in the panel where a field wire lands?
options: The wiring diagram or terminal schedule
The block diagram of the whole production system
The architect's floor plan of the building
The single-line diagram of the incoming supply

questions.stem: Every control wire in a panel has a ferrule with a number on it. How does this help fault finding?
options: It shows how many years each wire has been in service
It shows the current that each wire is designed to carry
It links each wire to the same number on the drawing
It shows which electrician fitted each wire and when

questions.stem: The instructor runs a faulty training board so that you can see the fault. What must happen before you test it?
options: Test the control circuit quickly while it is still running
Open the panel door and look inside with the supply still on
It is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead
Switch off the control fuse only and then start testing

questions.stem: A relay's changeover contact has terminals marked 11, 12 and 14. Which pair is normally closed?
options: A1–A2

questions.stem: On a thermal overload relay, which contact pair is usually the normally closed trip contact wired into the control circuit?
options: A1–A2

questions.stem: A motor starts when the start button is pressed, but stops as soon as the button is released. Which part is most likely at fault?
options: The stop button, which has stuck in the open position
The holding (latching) contact or its wiring
The heater element inside the overload relay
The main isolator feeding the motor starter

questions.stem: Two identical 24 V relay coils of 480 Ω each are connected in parallel. With the circuit isolated, what should a resistance reading across the pair show?
options: 0 Ω

questions.stem: Two identical 480 Ω coils should be in parallel, but the reading across them is 480 Ω. What is the most likely fault?
options: Both of the coils have shorted turns inside them
Both coils are good and the reading is correct
One coil or its wire is open circuit
The meter's battery is giving too much voltage

questions.stem: A 220 V contactor coil reads 0.2 Ω on a resistance test, with the leads nulled. What does this suggest?
options: The coil is in good order and can stay in service
The coil is shorted and must be replaced
The coil is open circuit and has no path at all
The coil needs a higher supply voltage to work

questions.stem: Why is one side of a control transformer's secondary usually connected to earth?
options: To double the voltage available to the control circuit
To make the contactor coils run cooler in hot weather
So that the control transformer needs no fuse at all
So an earth fault blows the fuse instead of starting the machine

questions.stem: Why must the secondary of a current transformer (CT) never be open-circuited while its primary carries current?
options: The energy meter connected to it will read backwards
The current in the primary conductor will stop flowing
The transformer's core will cool down too quickly
A dangerously high voltage can appear across it

questions.stem: Before a meter is disconnected from CT secondary wiring, the primary circuit is isolated. What else is usually fitted at the test block, as the procedure says?
options: A larger fuse in each of the CT secondary wires
A shorting link across the CT secondary
A capacitor across each of the meter terminals
A second meter wired in series with the first

questions.stem: A control circuit has eight devices in series between the fuse and a coil, and the coil does not pull in. With the circuit isolated, which method finds the open contact quickest?
options: Replace each device one at a time until the circuit works
Test every device in turn, starting from the coil end
Test at the middle, then at the middle of the faulty half
Shake each wire in turn to see which one is loose

questions.stem: A fault appears only when the panel gets hot in the afternoon. Which cause should you suspect first?
options: A loose or high-resistance joint
A wrong number printed on a wire ferrule
A coil rated for a higher voltage than the supply
Drawings that are a year or two out of date

questions.stem: A terminal shows signs of heating, and a resistance test across that joint reads higher than the others. What is the right repair?
options: Spray it with contact cleaner and leave it in service
Remake it with a new ferrule or lug, cleaned and torqued
Wrap insulating tape tightly round the whole terminal
Fit a larger fuse in the circuit to stop it blowing

questions.stem: How should fine-stranded control wire be prepared for a screw terminal?
options: Fit a crimped bootlace (cord-end) ferrule
Twist the strands and coat the end with solder
Fold the strands back over the insulation for grip
Cut some strands off so that it fits the terminal

questions.stem: A 24 V DC relay coil has a diode fitted across it. What is the diode's job?
options: To make the relay pull in more quickly
To change the DC supply into AC for the coil
To light up when the relay is switched on
To absorb the voltage spike when the coil switches off

questions.stem: Before an insulation resistance test on a control panel's wiring, what must be done?
options: Switch on the control supply so the relays pull in
Remove the number ferrules from each of the wires
Disconnect electronic parts such as controller cards and sensors
Connect every control wire in the panel to the earth bar

questions.stem: A 24 V DC solenoid draws 1 A at the end of a control cable. The loop (out and back) is 100 m of conductor at 0.02 Ω per metre. What is the voltage drop in the cable?
options: 1 V
4 V
2 V

questions.stem: A solenoid valve at the end of a long run hums but does not open, and the authorised person found the voltage at the coil low. What is a likely cause to check, dead?
options: The valve body was painted with the wrong kind of paint
The numbers on the wire ferrules have faded in the sun
The control fuse is a larger size than the drawing shows
A high-resistance joint or undersized cable

questions.stem: Forward and reverse contactors are wired so that each one's NC auxiliary contact is in the other's coil circuit. What is this for?
options: So both contactors can never close at once
So both directions can run together at full speed
So the motor needs no overload relay at all
So the motor stops whenever the door is opened

questions.stem: A star-delta starter stays in star and never changes over to delta. Which part is the most likely fault?
options: The main isolator feeding the whole starter panel
The timer or its changeover contact
The motor's protective earth connection
The stop button on the front of the panel

questions.stem: A sliding gate does not stop at its open position and runs on until its overload trips. What should you check first, with it isolated?
options: The open limit switch and its wiring
The colour code of the gate motor cable
The size of the main breaker in the building
The earth rod outside the building

questions.stem: A machine's proximity sensor is thought to be faulty. What is a safe way to confirm it?
options: Bridge the sensor's output wires so that the machine runs
Fit a known-good sensor of the same type; the authorised person tests
Bend the sensor's bracket until the machine starts to run
Cut its cable and twist the wires together to test it

questions.stem: Why must a safety circuit, such as a guard switch, never be bridged out to keep a machine running?
options: Bridging it makes the control voltage rise
Bridging it cancels the maker's paint warranty
The guard would no longer protect anyone
Bridging it stops the controller showing alarms

questions.stem: A control fuse has blown three times in a week. Each time it was replaced and the machine ran again. What should happen now?
options: Fit a fuse of twice the rating so it stops blowing
Keep replacing the fuse each time it blows
Bridge the fuse holder with a piece of copper wire
Find the root cause, such as a chafed wire

questions.stem: A control wire is found chafed through where it crosses a panel door hinge. What is the right repair?
options: Tape over the damage and leave the wire where it was
Cut the wire shorter so that it is pulled tight
Glue the wire to the door with silicone sealant
Replace it with flexible wire, protected at the hinge

questions.stem: A failed 24 V DC relay must be replaced. The store has a 220 V AC relay that fits the same base. What should you do?
options: Fit it, because if the base fits it will work
Fit it, and add a resistor in series with the coil
Get a relay with the same coil voltage and contact rating
Fit it, and change the control transformer to suit

questions.stem: During a repair, a spare contact is used in place of a burnt one, so the wiring changes. What must be done?
options: Nothing, as long as the machine now works properly
Mark up the drawing and update the wire labels
Tell the operator so that they can remember it
Take the old drawing out of the panel pocket

questions.stem: After a repair to a control circuit, which comes first?
options: Dead tests and checks of the connections
Switching on and pressing every button quickly
Handing it to the operator to try it out
Closing the panel and writing up the report

questions.stem: The repaired circuit passes its dead tests. Who carries out the function test with the supply on, at the Centre?
options: Any trainee in the group who is free at the time
The instructor, with the trainees standing clear
The trainee who made the repair, working alone
Nobody, because the dead tests are enough

questions.stem: A machine's fault history shows the same contactor has failed four times this year. What does this suggest?
options: The contactor's maker always makes poor parts
The operators are pressing the start button too hard
The fault history has probably been filled in wrongly
A root cause, such as wrong size, heat or frequent starts

questions.stem: Before using an ohmmeter on an isolated circuit, why do you set the right range and null the leads?
options: To make the meter's battery last longer
So the circuit can be energised safely
So small resistances are read correctly
So the meter can be used on live parts

questions.stem: Why is control wiring kept apart from power wiring inside a panel?
options: To reduce interference and make faults easier to trace
So the control wires can be thinner than the drawing allows
So the panel door closes without catching any cables
So no earth connection is needed on the control side

questions.stem: A two-way switched stair light works from one switch but not from the other. Which fault is most likely?
options: The lamp has blown and must be replaced
The breaker for the circuit is the wrong size
A strapper (traveller) is open or wrongly connected
The earth conductor is missing at the lamp

questions.stem: A 110 V radial socket circuit has five outlets, wired in order. Only the last two do not work. With the circuit isolated, where is the fault most likely?
options: At outlet three, or between it and outlet four
At the breaker for the circuit in the panel
At the first outlet on the circuit, near the panel
In the main earthing conductor at the meter

questions.stem: A GFCI (RCD) trips at random. Insulation resistance tests on the fixed wiring are good. What should you check next?
options: Fit a larger breaker in place of the GFCI
Test the connected appliances one at a time
Remove the earth connection from the circuit
Change the panel cover for a new one

questions.stem: A GFCI (RCD) trips as soon as it is reset, even with all loads unplugged. A dead test shows the neutral and earth joined in a junction box. What is this fault called?
options: An open circuit on the line conductor
An overload on the final circuit
A high-resistance joint in the line
A neutral-to-earth fault

questions.stem: You lead two trainees fault-finding on a board. One wants to change parts until it works. How do you guide them?
options: Ask them to say what each test shows before changing anything
Let them carry on, since changing parts finds the fault in the end
Do the job yourself quickly while they both stand and watch
Tell them to order every part shown on the drawing

questions.stem: A trainee's entry on a control panel's repair record must let the next electrician understand the job. Which entry does this best?
options: Machine was broken, so fixed it and it now runs
Contactor was bad, so it was changed for another one
Problem was found and was repaired as needed
K2 coil open circuit; replaced like for like; tests passed

questions.stem: You find a burnt terminal block, but the spare will not arrive until tomorrow. What should you do?
options: Join the wires with tape and run the machine until then
Leave it isolated, tagged out of service, and report it
Bridge across the terminal with a short piece of wire
Tell the operator to run the machine slowly for a day

questions.stem: A client asks how long a repair will take. What should your estimate be based on?
options: A quick guess, to keep the client happy for now
The time the last electrician took on another job
The fault found, the parts needed and delivery times
The longest time possible, so you are always safe

questions.stem: Why should the operator see the repaired machine working before you leave?
options: So the operator can learn to do the repair next time
So they can confirm it works as they need, and raise concerns
So the operator can sign for every part that was used
So you can charge the client for the extra time on site

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A 24 V relay coil reads 600 Ω. What current does it draw, in milliamps?
Three identical 600 Ω coils are connected in parallel. What resistance, in ohms, should be read across them with the circuit isolated?
What is the name of the contact that keeps a contactor's coil energised after the start button is released?
What is the name of the small printed sleeve fitted on a control wire to show its wire number?
A 24 V DC solenoid coil has a resistance of 48 Ω. What current does it draw, in amps?
In metering and protection wiring, what do the letters CT stand for?
What is the name for a joint that is not fully open but has too much resistance, so it heats up?
What is the name of the diagram that shows a control circuit as rungs drawn between two upright supply lines?
A solenoid is fed through a cable whose loop (out and back) is 120 m of conductor. Each metre has a resistance of 0.025 Ω. What is the total loop resistance, in ohms?
What is the name of the fault-finding method of swapping a suspect part for one known to be good?
On a contact, what do the letters NC stand for?
In a two-way lighting circuit, what is the name of a wire that links the two switches? Give one name.
What is the name of the method that keeps asking 'why?' until the real cause of a fault is found?
What is the name for a drawing that has been marked up to show how the wiring really is after changes were made?
Which instrument is used, with the circuit isolated, to measure the resistance of a coil or across a contact?

essays.stem: Describe a systematic method you would lead for finding a fault on a machine's control circuit, from the first report to handing the machine back.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by gathering information: what the operator saw, when the fault happens, any alarms, and the machine's fault history. I would get the latest schematic and wiring diagrams. If seeing the fault helps, the authorised person runs the machine while we watch from a safe place. Then the machine is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead with a tester checked before and after. Using the schematic, I would work out which part of the circuit could cause that symptom, so we test only that area. With dead tests, using an ohmmeter and operating switches by hand, we check each device and wire in turn, often by the half-split method. When the faulty part is found, I would ask why it failed, so the root cause is fixed and not just the symptom. The repair is made like for like, then dead tests are done, the authorised person runs a function test, the drawings are marked up if anything changed, and the fault report is written before handover.
markingPoints: Gathers information from operator, history and drawings
Isolates, locks off, tags and proves dead with a checked tester
Uses the schematic to narrow down the area and tests logically (e.g. half-split)
Finds and fixes the root cause with a like-for-like repair
Dead tests, function test by the authorised person, drawings updated and report written

essays.stem: Explain how a stop/start motor starter circuit with a holding contact and an overload relay works. Then describe the dead tests you would use to find the fault when (a) the motor stops as soon as start is released, and (b) the contactor will not pull in at all.
essays.modelAnswer: The control supply passes through a fuse, the overload relay's NC contact (95–96), the NC stop button and the NO start button to the contactor coil (A1–A2). Pressing start energises the coil, and the contactor closes its main contacts and an NO auxiliary holding contact wired across the start button. When start is released, current keeps flowing through the holding contact, so the motor keeps running until stop is pressed or the overload trips. For fault (a), the holding path has failed. With the circuit isolated, I would push the contactor closed by hand (if the maker allows) or use the test position and check continuity across the auxiliary contact, then check the wires from it to each side of the start button. For fault (b), I would check the fuse, then test continuity through 95–96, the stop button and the start button pressed, then measure the coil resistance: open circuit means a broken coil, near zero means a shorted coil.
markingPoints: Explains the series path: fuse, overload NC, stop NC, start NO, coil
Explains the holding contact across the start button
Fault (a): tests the holding contact and its wiring to the start button
Fault (b): tests fuse, overload contact, stop and start buttons in turn
Measures the coil and explains open and shorted readings; all dead tests

essays.stem: Explain the dangers of working on current transformer (CT) secondary wiring for a meter or protection relay, and describe how the work is made safe.
essays.modelAnswer: A CT steps a large primary current down to a small secondary current that drives a meter or relay. The secondary is meant to have a meter or a short across it at all times. If the secondary is opened while the primary carries current, the CT tries to push its current through the gap and can produce a very high voltage, which can give a fatal shock, cause arcing and damage the CT. The safest way is to isolate the primary circuit, lock it off and prove it dead, so no current flows in the CT at all. The secondary is also shorted at the test block or terminal block with the shorting links, as the procedure and drawings say, before any meter or relay wire is disconnected. Wires are labelled, the work is done, and the links are removed only after the meter or relay is reconnected and checked. The work is recorded and the authorised person restores the supply.
markingPoints: Explains what a CT does and that its secondary must always have a path
Explains the high voltage danger when the secondary is opened
Isolates, locks off and proves dead the primary circuit
Shorts the secondary at the test block before disconnecting, as the procedure says
Labels, reconnects, removes links only afterwards, records, and the authorised person restores the supply

essays.stem: Intermittent faults are among the hardest to find. Explain the common causes in Jamaican conditions and how you would track one down.
essays.modelAnswer: An intermittent fault comes and goes, so the circuit often tests good when you look at it. Common causes are loose or high-resistance terminals that open when hot, vibration from machines loosening connections or breaking wires, damp and salt air causing corrosion on contacts and terminals, especially near the coast, insects or lizards getting into panels, and chafed cables that touch earth only when something moves. Heat in a panel in the afternoon sun can make a weak part fail. To track one down, I would study the fault history for a pattern, such as time of day, weather or one machine operation. With the panel isolated and proved dead, I would inspect closely for discolouration, corrosion and loose wires, check terminal tightness and do resistance and insulation resistance tests, moving cables while testing. If needed I would ask the operator to log each event or use a recording device fitted by the authorised person. I would fix the cause and keep watching after the repair.
markingPoints: Explains what an intermittent fault is
Names common causes: loose or hot joints, vibration, corrosion from damp or salt, pests, chafed cables
Looks for patterns in the history
Inspects and dead-tests with the circuit isolated, moving cables during tests
Uses logging or monitoring if needed, fixes the cause and follows up

essays.stem: Describe the standard of workmanship you expect when your team repairs secondary wiring in a control panel.
essays.modelAnswer: Every repair must leave the panel at least as good as it was built. Replacement parts are like for like: the same coil voltage, contact rating and type, or an approved equal. Wire is the same size, colour and insulation type as the drawing gives. Fine-stranded wire is fitted with crimped bootlace ferrules, and terminals are tightened to the maker's torque. Each wire carries its number ferrule at both ends, matching the drawing. Wires are routed in the trunking, kept apart from power wiring, supported, and protected with flexible conduit or spiral wrap where they cross a door hinge. No safety device is ever bridged out. Spare cores are labelled and made safe. Any change from the original is marked up on the drawing and kept in the panel. The repair is dead-tested, then function-tested by the authorised person, and recorded.
markingPoints: Like-for-like parts and wire size, colour and type
Bootlace ferrules and correct torque
Wire numbers matching the drawing at both ends
Neat routing, segregation, support and hinge protection; no bypassing safety devices
Drawings marked up, tested and recorded

essays.stem: A GFCI (RCD) protecting the outdoor sockets and pool lights at a villa in Negril trips several times a week. Explain how you would find the cause, using dead tests only.
essays.modelAnswer: I would ask the owner when it trips: after rain, at night, or when a certain appliance is used. Then I would isolate the circuit at the board, lock off, tag and prove dead with a tester checked before and after. I would unplug all appliances and disconnect the pool light transformer and any electronic loads. I would carry out an insulation resistance test on the fixed wiring, line and neutral together to earth, and also neutral to earth separately, because a neutral touching earth can trip a GFCI. If a reading is low, I would split the circuit at junction boxes and outlets to find the section, looking for water in outdoor boxes, damaged cables or corroded fittings, which are common in salt air. If the wiring is good, I would test each appliance's insulation separately. Once found, the faulty part is repaired or replaced with suitably rated outdoor parts, retested, and the GFCI is tested by the authorised person after the supply is restored. I would record the findings.
markingPoints: Gathers information about when it trips
Isolates, locks off, tags and proves dead; disconnects loads and electronics
Insulation resistance tests including neutral to earth
Splits the circuit to locate low readings; checks outdoor boxes for water and corrosion; tests appliances
Repairs with suitable outdoor parts, retests, GFCI tested by the authorised person, records

essays.stem: A control fuse on a water pump keeps blowing. Using the 'five whys', show how you would find the root cause, and write the main points of the fault report.
essays.modelAnswer: Why did the fuse blow? Because there was a short circuit to earth on the control circuit. Why was there a short? Because a control wire's insulation had worn through where it touches the panel door edge. Why had it worn through? Because the wire was not protected or supported where it crosses the door, so it rubs each time the door opens. Why was it not protected? Because a past repair replaced the wire and left it loose. Why was it left loose? Because there was no check of workmanship after repairs. The root cause is a lack of a repair standard and checking, not the fuse. The report would give the machine and date, the symptom (fuse blowing), the tests and findings (insulation resistance low on wire 14, chafed at the hinge), the repair (wire replaced, protected and supported, fuse renewed at the same rating), the tests after repair, and the actions to stop it again (a workmanship check after every panel repair), signed by the person who did it.
markingPoints: Uses a chain of 'why' questions in a logical order
Reaches a root cause beyond the blown fuse
Report gives machine, date and symptom
Report gives tests, findings, repair and tests after repair
Report gives actions to prevent a repeat and is signed

essays.stem: You lead a team of three on a breakdown in a busy factory. Production is waiting. Explain how you would keep the work safe, quick and well recorded.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first speak to the supervisor and operator to understand the fault and the pressure on production, and give a realistic estimate once I knew more. I would make it clear that safety steps are never skipped to save time. One team member collects the drawings and history while another prepares the isolation; the machine is isolated with a group lock-off, each member fitting their own lock, and proved dead with a checked tester. I would share out the tests by area so we work in parallel, but each person tells me what they find, so we follow the evidence and do not change parts at random. When the cause is found, one person repairs while another checks spare parts and records. I would check the repair myself before covers go on, then the dead tests are done and the authorised person runs the function test. I would keep production informed, and write the fault report and update the history and drawings before leaving.
markingPoints: Gets information and gives the client a realistic estimate
Never skips safety: group lock-off and proving dead
Shares tasks so the team works efficiently but follows the evidence
Checks the repair, dead tests and function test by the authorised person
Keeps production informed and completes the report, history and drawings

essays.stem: A 24 V DC circuit has two relay coils, K1 and K2, of 480 Ω each, connected in parallel and fed through a fuse and a closed selector switch. With the supply isolated, explain the resistance readings you expect at each part of the circuit, and what readings would show (a) an open wire to K2 and (b) a shorted K1 coil.
essays.modelAnswer: With the circuit isolated, the fuse should read close to 0 Ω across it, and the selector switch should also read close to 0 Ω when closed and open circuit when open. Across the two coils in parallel, the expected reading is 480 × 480 ÷ (480 + 480) = 240 Ω, because two equal resistances in parallel give half the value. Each coil on its own should read about 480 Ω. (a) If the wire to K2 is open, current can only flow through K1, so the reading across the pair rises to about 480 Ω, and a reading taken across K2 at its own terminals is still 480 Ω, which shows the break is in the wire, not the coil. (b) If K1's coil is shorted, the reading across the pair falls close to 0 Ω, because the short is in parallel with K2. That fault would also blow the fuse when energised. In each case I would null the meter leads first and disconnect one end of a coil to test it on its own.
markingPoints: Fuse and closed switch read near 0 Ω; open switch reads open circuit
Calculates 240 Ω for the parallel pair and 480 Ω for each coil
Open wire to K2: pair reads about 480 Ω; K2 alone still 480 Ω, so the fault is the wire
Shorted K1: pair reads near 0 Ω and the fuse would blow
Nulls leads and disconnects one end to test parts on their own

essays.stem: Explain how a two-way lighting circuit works, and describe how you would find the fault when the light works from only one of the two switches.
essays.modelAnswer: In a two-way circuit, the line goes to the common terminal of the first switch. Two strappers (travellers) connect the two other terminals of the first switch to the matching terminals of the second switch. The common of the second switch feeds the lamp, and the neutral goes straight to the lamp. Each switch selects one strapper or the other, so changing either switch can complete or break the path. If the light works from only one switch, one strapper is usually open, or a strapper and a common have been swapped at one switch. With the circuit isolated, locked off and proved dead, I would take the switch plates off and identify the common at each switch from the marking. I would test continuity of each strapper from switch to switch, then check each switch by measuring from common to each strapper terminal in both positions. I would correct the broken or wrongly connected wire, retest, and ask the authorised person to check it works from both switches.
markingPoints: Explains the line to common, two strappers between switches, common to lamp
Explains why either switch can change the lamp
Names likely causes: an open strapper or a swapped common and strapper
Isolates, proves dead and tests strapper continuity and the switch positions
Corrects, retests, and the authorised person confirms operation

practical1.title: Diagnose and repair planted faults on a reversing starter panel with secondary wiring, and write a fault report
practical1.brief: The assessor sets up a training control panel with a forward/reverse starter, interlocks, an overload relay, a timer and pilot lamps, wired with numbered ferrules to a drawing. The assessor plants three faults in the control (secondary) wiring, for example an open holding contact wire, a missing interlock link and a wrong timer connection. The instructor runs the panel on its protected supply so the group can see the symptoms from a safe distance, then switches off. As a group: (1) record each symptom and, using the schematic, list the possible causes for each; (2) isolate the panel, every member fits a personal lock to a hasp, and the leader proves dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after; (3) find each fault with dead tests (ohmmeter, operating devices by hand) using a planned method such as half-split, recording each reading; (4) repair each fault to the drawing, with bootlace ferrules, number ferrules and correct torque; (5) do dead tests on the repaired circuit and record them; (6) the instructor carries out the function test while the group watches from a safe distance; (7) mark up the drawing if anything changed, and write a fault report with symptom, tests, cause, repair and prevention. Each member leads the diagnosis of at least one fault and makes at least one repair. Photograph each stage and hand in the test notes, marked-up drawing and report.
materials: Training control panel with forward/reverse starter, interlocks, overload, timer and pilot lamps (protected supply, switched only by the instructor)
Schematic and wiring diagram of the panel
Multimeter or ohmmeter, two-pole voltage tester and proving unit
Hasp, a padlock and tag for each member
Control wire, bootlace ferrules and crimper, number ferrules
Screwdrivers, torque screwdriver, strippers and side cutters
Fault-finding record sheet and fault report form
photos: The symptom list and possible causes written against the schematic
The hasp with every member's lock, and proving dead
A test being made, with the reading recorded
Each fault after repair, showing ferrules and neat wiring
The dead test record after repair
The marked-up drawing and the completed fault report
checklist: Linked each symptom to possible causes using the schematic
Fitted their own lock and followed safe isolation, proving dead with the tester checked before and after
Used a logical test method and recorded readings
Correctly found the fault they led
Repaired to the drawing with bootlace ferrules, number ferrules and correct torque
Carried out dead tests after repair and stood clear during the instructor's function test
Wrote a clear report section with cause and prevention
safety: Only the instructor energises the panel; all testing by trainees is done dead
Stand clear behind the marked line whenever the instructor runs the panel
Never bridge out an interlock, overload or stop circuit
Wear safety glasses when cutting and crimping wire

practical2.title: Trace and correct faults on a multi-circuit training installation, then retest and certify it
practical2.brief: The assessor sets up a training bay with a small distribution board feeding a two-way lighting circuit, a 110 V radial socket circuit with four outlets, a 220 V circuit to a fixed heater shell, and a GFCI (RCD) protected outdoor socket. The bay is never connected to a supply during the task. The assessor plants four faults, for example a broken strapper, a high-resistance joint at a socket, a neutral-to-earth fault in a junction box and a loose earth at the heater. The assessor gives each fault as a customer complaint. As a group: (1) read the complaints and plan which tests will find each fault; (2) isolate the bay at its board, lock off, tag and prove dead with a tester checked before and after; (3) carry out continuity, insulation resistance (including neutral to earth) and polarity tests to locate each fault, splitting circuits at boxes where needed; (4) repair each fault properly, with like-for-like parts and correct torque; (5) retest every circuit and complete a schedule of test results; (6) write a short report for the 'customer' explaining each fault in plain words. Each member leads the search for one fault and completes part of the test schedule. Photograph each stage and hand in the test schedule and report.
materials: Training bay with distribution board, two-way lighting, radial sockets, fixed heater shell and GFCI-protected outdoor socket (not connected to any supply)
Customer complaint cards from the assessor
Low-resistance ohmmeter and insulation resistance tester
Two-pole voltage tester and proving unit, lock, hasp and tags
Spare connectors, a socket outlet and cable
Schedule of test results and report forms
photos: The test plan written against each complaint
The board locked off and tagged, and proving dead
Each fault found, with the test reading
Each repair before covers are refitted
The completed schedule of test results
checklist: Chose the right test for each complaint
Isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead correctly
Carried out insulation resistance tests correctly, including neutral to earth, with loads disconnected
Located the fault they led by splitting the circuit logically
Repaired faults with suitable parts and correct torque
Recorded retest results accurately on the schedule
Explained the faults clearly in plain words
safety: The bay is never connected to a supply; only the instructor may energise anything
Discharge circuits after insulation resistance tests and warn others before testing
Keep the board locked off until all work and tests are complete
Wear safety glasses when stripping cable
